Excellent investigative reporting by Tom Latchem, Will Neal, and Pablo Manríquez, published by PunchUp and Migrant Insider. Essential reading on how the U.S. is exporting deportation infrastructure beyond its borders. Read the full piece:

thepunchup.substack.com/p/tr…

The same platform would connect to ONPAR, Panama's asylum office, so the deportation system and the refugee protection system share one backbone. Sharma-Crawford reads it as a template. "I think this is the master plan for global implementation," she said.

What is new is the data. The platform would feed Panama's system into U.S. screening tools and a biometric repository of more than 300 million identities. Geographer Louise Amoore calls this the biometric border, a border that travels with the body itself.

A migrant who does not appeal or claim fear of return within five days is advanced automatically to removal. Immigration attorney Rekha Sharma-Crawford called it unworkable. "This window is not really a window," she said. "It's more like a trap door."

The Panama documents push this further. DHS describes a system it designed, built, funded, and can log into, operated on the ground by Panama's migration service, moving a migrant from first encounter to deportation flight in as little as five days.

The U.S. has its own record. Remain in Mexico kept asylum seekers across the border. The 2019 agreements with Guatemala, Honduras, and El Salvador routed migrants to seek protection there. Last year Panama began taking deportees the U.S. could not easily return.

A second mechanism is offshore processing. Australia has held asylum seekers on Nauru for years. The UK pursued a plan to send them to Rwanda. Geographer Alison Mountz calls this an "enforcement archipelago" built to shrink the spaces where asylum is reachable.

One mechanism is to pay a buffer state. The EU gave Turkey roughly 6 billion euros to hold Syrian refugees, and funds and trains Libya's coast guard to intercept boats and return people to detention. The interdiction happens far from European soil.

Legal scholar Ayelet Shachar describes a "shifting border" that detaches from the territorial edge and follows the migrant outward. The border becomes a function carried by visas, funding, data, and foreign police, reaching wherever a journey begins.

The idea has a name in the research. Political scientist Aristide Zolberg called it "remote control." David FitzGerald's book Refuge Beyond Reach shows how rich democracies design deterrence so asylum seekers never reach the territory where protection obligations apply.

Wealthy democracies have spent two decades moving their borders outward, paying other countries to stop migrants long before they reach the actual line. Scholars call it border externalization. A new DHS plan for Panama is the latest example. 🧵
